title: Origin of eukaryotic cells
summary: Eukaryotic cells have a nucleus, a sophisticated endomembrane system and mitochondria, the last from an ancient endosymbiosis with a proteobacterium. Probable eukaryote fossils, spherical acritarchs, appear about 1.8 billion years ago, and the prevailing view places the last common ancestor of eukaryotes by 1.6 to 1.8 billion years ago. How this complex cell evolved is still a puzzle, partly because few living intermediates remain.

uncertainty.note: Estimated from early acritarch microfossil records (~1.8 Ga) and crown-group eukaryote divergence windows (1.8–1.6 Ga) reviewed by Porter (2020) and UCMP Berkeley.

as_recorded.value: More probable eukaryote fossils begin to appear at about 1.8 billion years ago. These are spherical fossils of likely algal protists, called acritarchs
The prevailing view of the early eukaryote fossil record is that LECA appeared by 1.6–1.8 Ga

when.display: c. 1.8–1.6 billion years ago (Late Paleoproterozoic to early Mesoproterozoic)

where.modern_name: No single place; stand-in pin at Negaunee, Michigan, United States
where.historical_name: Not applicable (Late Paleoproterozoic oceans of supercontinent Nuna/Columbia; no modern polities or geographic features existed)

paleo.not_applicable: Deep time global biological evolutionary transition in Paleoproterozoic oceans across assembling supercontinent Columbia/Nuna.

importance.justification: Eukaryogenesis produced the complex cell architecture, organelles, and nucleus that founded all complex multicellular life including animals, plants, and fungi.

related.because: The primordial emergence of cellular life and prokaryotic diversification was the evolutionary prerequisite for endosymbiotic eukaryogenesis.
The rise of atmospheric and shallow-ocean oxygen provided the energetic basis for mitochondrial aerobic respiration in early eukaryotes.
Eukaryotic cellular complexity and endomembrane systems were necessary foundations for the evolution of complex multicellularity.
